name: Motivated forgetting
statement: Deliberately keeping a memory out of awareness when a reminder appears is claimed to make that memory harder to recall later.
meaning: Motivated forgetting is the umbrella term for forgetting produced by active processes rather than by time or interference. Anderson and Hanslmayr define it as increased forgetting arising from active processes that down-prioritise unwanted experiences in service of creating or sustaining an emotional or cognitive state. Two laboratory paradigms carry most of the weight, and they are different tasks. Directed forgetting attaches a forget or a remember instruction to material as it is studied, either item by item or to a whole list, so it acts on encoding. The think/no-think task trains cue and target to criterion first, then presents the cue and asks the person to keep the target out of mind. Only the second models the situation the clinical literature cares about, where a reminder arrives and the memory is unwelcome. The measure is recall of suppressed items against baseline items that were studied and then left alone. Testing with a cue that never appeared in the experiment, called an independent probe, is what separates damage to the memory itself from interference at the trained cue. The replication verdict below describes the think/no-think task and nothing else. Item-method directed forgetting is summarised here for contrast and has its own record. Retrieval-induced forgetting is a third paradigm with a third record, kept at entry 278. The clinical claim that trauma can be repressed and later recovered is a fourth argument, and no laboratory result settles it.

origin.who: Michael C. Anderson and Collin Green
origin.note: Anderson and Green's think/no-think experiments are what the current literature is built on, and their paper names Freud's repression as the hypothesis under test. The label is older. Glucksberg and King published a laboratory analogue of repression in Science in 1967 under the heading of motivated forgetting, Weiner and Higgins called that paradigm confounded in 1969, and Glucksberg and Ornstein replied in the same issue. Those three are described here from their titles and Crossref records and were not read. Anderson and Hanslmayr's 2014 review is the paper that gathers directed forgetting and retrieval suppression under the one term.

evidence: Anderson and Green ran four experiments. Thirty-two students took part in each of the first three and sixteen in the fourth. Each learned 40 critical word pairs and 10 filler pairs, drilled until at least half the pairs were recalled correctly. The think/no-think phase gave 377 trials. Respond cues stayed on screen for up to 4 s or until the answer came, suppression cues for the full 4 s, and saying a suppressed target set off a loud error beep. Five pairs sat in each of the 0, 1, 8 and 16 repetition conditions for both instructions, and the 0 condition was the baseline. Recall of suppressed items fell below baseline, and the drop grew with the number of suppression attempts, while recall of respond items rose. The caption to Figure 1 reports inhibition between 0 and 16 suppressions as significant at P < 0.01 in experiments 1 to 3, and at P < 0.05 in every same-probe and independent-probe test in those three. The independent probe supplied a category name and a first letter, insect r for the target roach, so the impairment could not be put down to interference at the trained cue. Experiment 2 paid 25 cents per correct answer up to $4 and the pattern held. Experiment 3 told participants that the researchers expected suppression to improve memory, a story they believed at a mean rating of 4.2 on a five-point scale, and the pattern held again. Experiment 4 dropped the instruction to control awareness and asked only that the answer not be spoken aloud. Recall did not decline with repetitions, F < 1 in all cases, and inhibition was reliably larger in experiments 1 to 3 than in experiment 4, P < 0.05. The article carries no table of condition means, so no recall percentage from the original is quoted here. Liu, Hulbert, Yang, Guo, Qiu and Anderson recruited 497 people across an fMRI study and a behavioural study, and 492 of them contributed to the forgetting analyses. Suppressed items were recalled worse than baseline items, F(1, 491) = 116.327, p < 0.001, in the unconditionalised data. Their questionnaire scores non-compliance rather than compliance, summing three questions about checking or rehearsing no-think targets, and forgetting shrank as that score rose, r = -0.209, 95% CI [-0.289, -0.135]. Test expectancy was not associated with forgetting. Nardo and Anderson's method paper puts typical suppression-induced forgetting at about 7 to 10%, counts more than a hundred published think/no-think studies whose large majority found the effect, and puts the failures at about a dozen. The directed-forgetting literature is larger and steadier. Hall, Fawcett, Hourihan and Fawcett identified 607 studies, kept 31 and modelled 36 effects with Bayesian multilevel models. Remember items beat forget items by 19.6%, CI95% [16.1, 23.1], for neutral material and by 15.1%, CI95% [12.4, 17.7], for emotional material, a within-study gap of 4.2%, CI95% [2.0, 6.4]. They add that the gap varies broadly across studies and depends on methodological features. Pevie, Baldwin, Fawcett, Lahey and Fawcett screened 823 articles, kept 36, and found the directed-forgetting effect smaller in clinical than in control groups.

examples.text: Passing the hospital where a relative died, someone makes a habit of turning their thoughts elsewhere the moment the building appears. Months later the details of the last visit come back more slowly than other memories from the same weeks that were left alone.

A colleague's name arrives in the inbox most mornings, and each time it calls up something embarrassing said at a leaving do. Batting the scene away every time makes it harder to summon later than other scenes from the same evening.

A photograph of a former partner stays on the shelf, and every glance at it is met with deliberately thinking about something else. The argument it used to bring to mind arrives less readily after a few months of that, which is the suppression working rather than time passing.

replication.headline: Two meta-analyses find a small aggregate suppression effect, 0.28 across 25 studies and d of about 0.20 to 0.40 across 120, while a preregistered online replication of 150 people found d = 0.03.
replication.detail: Bulevich, Roediger, Balota and Butler ran three experiments modelled on Anderson and Green, with the same 1, 8 and 16 repetitions and the same two probe types, and analysed 32 people in each. In experiment 2 same-probe recall of suppressed items ran from .68 at baseline to .64 after 16 suppressions, t(31) = 1.29, and independent-probe recall from .78 to .76, t(31) = 0.62. None of the three experiments showed reliable suppression on either probe, and they concluded that suppression is not a robust phenomenon in the paradigm. Wessel, Albers, Zandstra and Heininga published two replications from the 2000s that had sat unpublished, N = 49 and N = 36, and reanalysed two of their own published studies, N = 68 and N = 80, running every defensible analysis in parallel. Same-probe suppression was significant across the whole multiverse in the N = 36 and N = 80 samples, mixed in the N = 68 sample and carried by a single test in the N = 49 sample. Independent-probe tests were predominantly non-significant, which they treat as a problem for inhibition theory and for repression as a mechanism of forgetting. Wiechert and six colleagues ran a preregistered online version with an experimenter present on a video call. Of 213 people who began the session, 150 were analysed. Neither probe gave the effect: same probe BF01 = 7.84, d = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.13, 0.20]; independent probe BF01 = 5.71, d = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.24]. Their compliance score was unrelated to either difference score, BF10 = 0.10 in both cases. Wessel, Lehmann and Wiechert then adapted that procedure for undergraduates. A first study screened 62 and analysed 54 in the laboratory, where no-think recall of 77.62% sat below baseline recall of 85.80%, t(53) = 3.52, Cohen's d = 0.59, 95% CI [0.23, 0.95], BF10 = 60.65. A second study screened 129 and analysed 54 in the laboratory and 54 online. The laboratory arm gave d = 0.42, 95% CI [0.16, 0.69], BF10 = 32.49. The online arm gave d = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.30, 0.41], BF01 = 5.11. They report conclusive evidence for a null online without evidence that the two settings themselves differed, and read the pair as casting doubt on how far the effect generalises. On the other side, Liu and colleagues found the effect in 492 analysed participants. Stramaccia, Meyer, Rischer, Fawcett and Benoit pooled 96 effects from 25 studies and give 0.28, 95% CI [0.14, 0.43], for healthy participants, as a standardised mean change rather than a d. The same models give -0.21, CI [-0.41, -0.02], for more anxious people, 0.05, CI [-0.19, 0.29], for depressed people, and 0.42, CI [0.32, 0.52], for people with a repressive coping style. Instructions moved the estimate more than anything else: 0.66, CI [0.42, 0.90], for direct retrieval suppression, 0.59, CI [0.40, 0.77], for thought substitution, and -0.02, CI [-0.29, 0.26], where the instruction was left unspecified. Their abstract says the healthy estimate may be inflated by publication bias. Their results section reports Egger's regression as non-significant at p = .182, and a trim-and-fill penalty that grew when unpublished null and reversed studies were included. Clark, Todorovic, Levy, Eschmann, Klein, Anderson, van Schie, Whitridge, Yick and Fawcett published a larger meta-analysis in 2026. Its abstract reports 500 effects from 120 studies and a consistent aggregate effect of d about 0.20 to 0.40, with forgetting of about 6% on same probes, 5 to 6% on independent probes and 2 to 4% on recognition. It also reports considerable methodological variability and prediction intervals showing substantial heterogeneity. The dispute has an answer scheduled. Fawcett, Levy, Bergström, Bulevich, Clark, Hertel, Hulbert, MacLeod, Todorovic, van Schie and the Memory Control Consortium hold an acceptance in principle for a multisite replication. The registered sample is 3,984 participants, 1,992 in each instruction condition, spread across 78 contributing groups, with collection running between that acceptance and 1 April 2024. The protocol says it chose not to replicate the 2001 report directly, because the task has undergone numerous methodological changes since, and it powers the design to detect d of about 0.15. Searches of Crossref, PubMed and Europe PMC on 21 September 2026 returned no Stage 2 report.

study.cite: Wiechert, S., Loewy, L., Wessel, I., Fawcett, J. M., Ben-Shakhar, G., Pertzov, Y., & Verschuere, B. (2023). Suppression-induced forgetting: a pre-registered replication of the think/no-think paradigm. Memory, 31(7), 989-1002.

limits: This entry covers the think/no-think paradigm and, for contrast, item-method directed forgetting. It does not cover retrieval-induced forgetting, which is entry 278, the neuroimaging work, Wegner's thought suppression, or children's memory. The search ran across Crossref, DataCite, PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, OSF and the open web on 21 September 2026. Three documents were not read in full. Wessel's review of independent-probe suppression is open access at Wiley under CC BY-NC, and Groningen holds the accepted version. Both hosts returned a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall on 21 September 2026, so the review was read in abstract at PubMed. Clark and colleagues' 2026 meta-analysis is closed at the American Psychological Association. Its abstract was read at PubMed and again at Europe PMC, and every figure quoted from it here comes from that abstract. A version 2 preprint carries the same figures, and the published article is the one cited. Stramaccia and colleagues' meta-analysis was read from the accepted manuscript at the Max Planck Society's repository, which states on its first page that it is not the copy of record. The green copy listed at the University of Luxembourg could not be reached at all, giving a certificate failure over HTTPS and a 503 over HTTP. A previous version of this page said that Taylor and Francis blocked the full texts of the Wessel multiverse paper and the Wiechert replication, and that both were read only in abstract. Both are open access and both were read in full for this revision, the multiverse paper from the KU Leuven repository and the replication from the University of Amsterdam repository. The 0.66 and 0.59 figures were previously quoted at one remove from the multisite protocol and have now been read in the meta-analysis itself. The two sources describe them differently. The protocol calls them Cohen's d and labels the first thought avoidance; the meta-analysis calls them standardised mean changes and labels the first direct retrieval suppression. Nardo and Anderson also print 0.66 as Cohen's d and call it large, where the meta-analysis calls it medium. Anderson and Green plot their condition means in Figures 1 and 3 and print no table of them, which is why no recall percentage from the original appears above. The paper describes a 16-repetition item as receiving about one minute of suppression in total. The paradigm uses neutral word pairs learned and tested in a single session. Hall and colleagues' percentages come from Bayesian multilevel models and their intervals are posterior intervals, which the paper labels CI95%. Wessel's review concludes that reliable estimates of the overall independent-probe effect size are unavailable, that the extent of publication and reporting bias is unknown, and that autobiographical memories are hard to study this way.
misreadings: Motivated forgetting and directed forgetting get treated as one result. Directed forgetting attaches its instruction to material as it is studied and acts on encoding. The think/no-think task trains the pair to criterion and then attacks retrieval when the cue returns. Anderson and Green drew the line themselves, writing that research into directed forgetting suggests a controllable inhibition process limited in scope to an immediately preceding temporal interval. The evidence behind the two is unequal. Item-method directed forgetting is a 19.6% recall difference for neutral material across 31 studies; suppression-induced forgetting aggregates to about 6% on same probes across 120 studies, with wide prediction intervals. A failed think/no-think study is then read as proof that nobody can forget on purpose. Liu and colleagues' result points at a duller explanation, which is that the no-think instruction often goes unfollowed. Wiechert and colleagues scored compliance the same way and found it unrelated to their null result, so that explanation is contested rather than established. Anderson and Green's paper is quoted as showing Freud was right. It offers itself as a model of repression, and Wessel's review of the independent-probe evidence concludes that it is a doubtful one. Whether trauma can be repressed and later recovered is a separate argument and still a live one. Otgaar, Howe, Patihis, Merckelbach, Lynn, Lilienfeld and Loftus aggregated survey samples totalling 4,745 respondents and put belief in repressed memories at 58%, rising to 70% among the 2,305 clinical psychologists in that pool and falling to 46% among the 2,063 laypeople. They caution that collapsing across surveys of different populations needs care. This page records what the laboratory task has and has not shown and takes no side on the clinical question. Motivated forgetting also runs the opposite way from this atlas's entries on false memory and suggestibility, which are about acquiring a memory of something that did not happen rather than losing access to one that did.
